TPU.d: Tensor Processing Unit: a chip Google designs specifically for the maths inside neural networks. Google trains and serves Gemini on TPUs and rents them to other companies, including Anthropic, through Google Cloud.

Mixture of Experts.d: A model design (often shortened to MoE) where the network contains many smaller 'expert' parts and a router sends each token to only a few of them. Announcements then quote two sizes: total parameters (all experts) and active parameters (the ones used per token).

Frontier model.d: One of the most capable AI models available at a given time, usually from a large lab such as Anthropic, OpenAI or Google DeepMind. The label is relative and changes as new models appear.

CUDA.d: NVIDIA's software platform (first released 2006–07) that lets programmers use NVIDIA GPUs for general computing. Most deep-learning software is built on it, which is a big reason NVIDIA dominates AI hardware.

Hyperscaler.d: A company that runs cloud computing at enormous scale, such as Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. Hyperscalers are the biggest buyers of AI chips and a main route by which companies reach AI models.

Model licence.d: The legal terms that say what you may do with a downloadable model: use it commercially, change it, redistribute it. Some are standard open-source licences (Apache 2.0, MIT); others are custom, with conditions you must read.

Sovereign AI.d: AI that a country or organisation can run and control within its own borders or infrastructure, rather than depending on a foreign provider's service. Often given as a reason to choose open-weight or locally hosted models.

Entity List.d: A US government list of foreign companies and organisations that face export restrictions, so US technology cannot be supplied to them without a licence. Some AI companies are on it, which can affect whether your employer may use their services.
